Lesser weever (Echiichthys vipera) is a small benthic scorpaeniform that inhabits sandy substrates of the northeastern Atlantic. This species reaches an ultimate total length of 27.7 centimeters [Li = 27.7 centimeters], a value that distinguishes it from the larger greater weever (Trachinus draco). Field surveys have demonstrated that age at birth is approximately 26 days [ab = approximately 26 days] when water temperatures are maintained at 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], a developmental duration that reflects the relatively slow embryonic metabolism characteristic of cooler-water spawning grounds. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae possess a wet weight at birth of only 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], a consequence of the small pelagic ova that measure roughly 1.3 millimeters in diameter. These lecithotrophic prolarvae depend entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-eclosion, and the initial body mass imposes a constraint on early survival under variable food availability.

Total length at puberty is approximately 6.27 centimeters [Lp = approximately 6.27 centimeters], a threshold that is reached well before the species attains its full somatic dimensions. Using length-weight regression parameters typical of trachinids, the corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 1.91 grams [Wwp = 1.91 grams]. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) in Echiichthys vipera, measured under laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], yielded a mean value of 8% [GSI = 8%]. This metric indicates that reproductive tissue accounts for approximately eight percent of total somatic mass during the peak spawning season, a figure that aligns with iteroparous spawning strategies among temperate demersal fishes.

Maximum recorded longevity for individuals maintained in captivity at 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C] reaches approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], a lifespan that is notably extended for a fish of modest body size. This remarkable longevity likely reflects the low metabolic costs associated with a sedentary, energy-conserving foraging mode and the absence of major piscine predators in its preferred habitat. The ultimate wet weight of 177.6 grams [Wwi = 177.6 grams] is attained gradually over many years of growth, with asymptotic mass being approached only after the majority of reproductive life has elapsed. Comparative data from other sand-dwelling scorpaeniforms suggest that such a prolonged growth trajectory is unusual and may be linked to the weever's reliance on venomous dorsal spines for predator deterrence, which reduces extrinsic mortality risk and allows selection to favor delayed senescence.

Reproductive investment in Echiichthys vipera exhibits a clear seasonal pattern, with gravid females depositing multiple demersal egg batches over the course of the spawning period. At a steady 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C], the gonadosomatic index reached 8% [GSI = 8%]. The onset of reproductive capacity in this species occurs at a remarkably consistent body length of 6.27 centimeters [Lp = 6.27 centimeters] throughout its distributional range. The mass at which gonadal maturation is attained, derived from trachinid length-mass regressions, is 1.91 grams [Wwp = 1.91 grams] in this species. Early maturation at a modest body mass is typical of species that experience moderate adult mortality and that benefit from rapid completion of the prereproductive growth period.

Many aspects of the weevers life history remain incompletely documented, particularly regarding the dynamics of somatic growth and the ecological correlates of its extended lifespan. Available evidence indicates that individuals may persist for as long as 15 years [am = 15 years] under the cool thermal conditions (10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]) characteristic of much of its range, an age that far exceeds the 5 to 7 year maxima estimated for most co-occurring sciaenids and pleuronectiforms. These data, though derived in part from comparative allometry with Trachinus draco, provide a coherent framework for understanding the trade-offs that govern growth, maturation, and reproductive scheduling in this venomous sand dweller.
